newsitem.title: USA: Stock funds lose steam as market skids.
newsitem.headline: Stock funds lose steam as market skids.

text.p: For the first time in more than two years, U.S. stock mutual funds lost value in the first quarter, as worries over a heated-up economy and higher interest rates sent the stock market skidding.
The average U.S. stock fund declined 1.98 percent, the first negative period since the fourth quarter of 1994, according to Lipper Analytical Services.
"Expectations were out of line in terms of earnings, cash flow and interest rates," said the firm's president, Michael Lipper.
"There were fewer buyers and increased sellers of underlying stocks in (fund) portfolios, and that would lead to the performance going down," Lipper said.

Lipper said domestic equity funds had declined since late January, if not earlier. "The volatility that marked the last weeks of the quarter may signal a change in the market's overall direction," said Lipper.

The hardest hit were small-cap funds, down 6.91 percent for the quarter; mid-cap, off 5.84 percent; micro-cap, falling 4.88 percent, and capital appreciation funds declined 3.26 percent, according to Lipper.
Index funds gained 2.52 percent; equity income rose 1.68 percent; and growth and income was up 1.13 percent.
The average science and technology fund dropped 8.60 percent, and growth funds fell 1.28 percent.
Japanese funds dropped 6.70 percent, and Canadian funds fell 6.59 percent.

Fund analysts said investors tightened their wallets as the quarter progressed. "Flows were heavy, with over $50 billion coming into equity funds in the first quarter," said Bob Adler, president of AMG Data Services. "But the rate of money coming into those funds steadily dropped throughout the quarter," he said.
The technology sector suffered the greatest redemptions beginning in mid-February and continuing until mid-March. The trend spilled over to the small-cap sector, Adler said.
The sell-off in tech funds roughly paralleled a decline in the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite index, which slid from a record close of 1,388 on Jan. 22 to about 1,200 on Wednesday.
For the entire quarter, Adler noted, redemptions in the technology sector were flat. There were no net redemptions over the quarter, he added.
Lipper noted that the general stock fund gained 10.82 percent over the past 12 months, which was in line with the historical 35-year average of 10.84 percent.

"I don't know why we couldn't finish this decade at that rate, assuming earnings keep going up, and there are no surprises," said Sheldon Jacobs, publisher of No Load Fund Investor. "If we have a war, then all bets are off."

The top five funds for the quarter were: American Heritage, up 48.21 percent; Lexington Troika Russia, up 46 percent; Merrill Middle East Africa, up 23.13 percent; Rembrandt Latin American Equity, up 17.29 percent; and Vontobel Eastern European, up 16.52 percent.

According to Lipper, the top five laggards included Calvert Strategic Growth, off 26.15 percent; Parkstone Small Cap Institutional, off 23.13 percent; PBHG Core Growth, off 22.14 percent; TCW/Dean Witter Small Cap Growth, off 21.22 percent; and TCW/Dean Witter Mid-Cap Equity, off 21.17 percent.
